title: DJ Basin Mineral Rights
metaTitle: Sell DJ Basin Mineral Rights | Colorado Niobrara/Codell
metaDescription: Own DJ Basin minerals in Weld, Adams, or Boulder County? We underwrite Niobrara and Codell spacing units and quote against your recent royalty checks.
heroLead: The DJ Basin is the most active horizontal play in Colorado, and it's also the most exposed to setback litigation and permitting delays that leave owners unsure what a check is actually worth.
intro: The Denver-Julesburg Basin runs under Weld, Adams, Morgan, Boulder, and Larimer counties, and it has been Colorado's dominant oil play since operators cracked the Niobrara and Codell benches with long horizontal laterals and dense pad development. Weld County alone hosts thousands of producing horizontals, most drilled from multi-well pads targeting stacked benches under a single spacing unit.

We buy and evaluate DJ Basin mineral and royalty interests every week, and the file we build looks the same whether the tract is core Weld County or the northern flank toward the Wyoming line: recent decline behavior, offset permits, and how far the tract sits from Greeley, Fort Lupton, or Platteville, where pad density is heaviest.

sections.heading: Where value concentrates in the DJ
paragraphs: Value in this basin is not flat across the map. Core Weld County acreage held by pads targeting the Niobrara B and C benches plus the Codell tends to price against a materially different decline curve than flank acreage in Adams or Morgan County, where laterals are shorter or spacing is thinner. We ask for your check stubs going back 12 to 24 months before we quote anything, because a DJ well's first-year decline is steep and a tract that looked strong two years ago may already be well into its tail production.

Undeveloped or leased-but-undrilled minerals in the DJ carry a different kind of value entirely, tied to permit backlog and where the operator sits in its multi-year development plan rather than to any check history. We look at COGCC permit filings and offset activity to judge how close a tract actually is to being drilled versus sitting in a queue.

sections.heading: Setback rules changed the math here first
paragraphs: Colorado's 2,000-foot setback rule from occupied structures, layered on top of local Weld and Adams County land use rules, has pushed some DJ development toward larger multi-well pads set back from platted subdivisions, and slowed permitting in areas closer to Denver's northern suburbs. That matters directly to owners: a tract that sits inside a growing subdivision footprint may see drilling delayed or redirected to a neighboring section, changing the timeline on when non-producing minerals start throwing off royalty.

We track which parts of Weld and Adams County are still seeing active permitting under current setback and local rules versus areas where suburban growth has effectively pushed operators elsewhere, and we build that into how we underwrite undrilled acreage.

sections.heading: Split estate is the norm, not the exception
paragraphs: A large share of DJ Basin minerals were severed from the surface decades ago through agricultural patents, oil and gas leases from the 1970s and 80s, or estate divisions that split the mineral estate among heirs while the surface stayed with a single farm or ranch owner. If your interest traces back to a family homestead near Greeley, Fort Morgan, or the Longmont area, there is a good chance you hold a split estate interest with a surface owner you have never met.

That structure affects access to records: the surface owner's lease file, the county clerk's recorded instruments, and the operator's division order desk are three separate sources, and reconciling them is part of what we do before we quote a number.

sections.heading: How pad density changes the underwriting
paragraphs: Modern DJ Basin development leans heavily on large multi-well pads, sometimes a dozen or more laterals drilled from a single surface location targeting several benches at once. That density is efficient for the operator but it also means your spacing unit may share drainage with more wells than an older single-well unit would, which spreads production across more interests and changes the per-acre revenue math over the life of the unit.

We check how many wells currently produce from your specific unit and whether the operator has filed for additional wells nearby, since a unit that's only partially developed today can see a meaningful step up in royalty once remaining laterals are drilled and turned to sales.

faqs.question: Is DJ Basin acreage still being permitted, or has development slowed?
faqs.answer: Both are true depending on where the tract sits. Core Weld County pad development continues, while some areas closer to Denver's northern suburbs have seen permitting slow under current setback and local land-use constraints. We check offset permit activity for your specific section before quoting.

faqs.question: How steep is the decline on a typical DJ horizontal?
faqs.answer: DJ Basin horizontals typically show a sharp first-year decline followed by a longer, shallower tail, which is why we ask for 12 to 24 months of check stubs rather than a single recent payment to build an accurate curve.

faqs.question: My minerals are non-producing near Fort Lupton. Does that mean they're worthless?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Non-producing DJ acreage in an active development corridor can carry real value tied to permit timing, even with no check history yet, though it prices differently than producing royalty.

faqs.question: Do I need to find the surface owner to sell my minerals?
faqs.answer: No. A severed mineral interest can be sold independently of the surface. We work directly from your recorded deed and the operator's division order records, not through the surface owner.
